introduction:
In recent years, the excessive and improper use of antibiotics has led to increasing antibiotic resistance of pathogenic bacteria. The development of antibiotic-resistance genes and multidrug resistance during bacterial evolution can greatly reduce the effectiveness of antibiotic treatments [1]. The escalation in the number of antibiotic-resistant bacterial isolates, accompanied by the bottlenecks in antibiotic discovery, has resulted in the resurgence of easy-treated diseases [2]. Consequently, antibiotic-resistant bacteria have emerged as a growing global health threat [3]. Meanwhile, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have emerged as a promising alternative to effectively combat antibiotic-resistant bacteria using unique antimicrobial mechanisms [4]. AMPs are a class of natural or synthetic peptide molecules. They are composed of short amino acid sequences, typically ranging from 10 to 50 amino acids. These peptides are widely distributed in nature. AMPs represent a crucial defense mechanism that organisms have developed through evolution [5]. Unlike traditional antibiotics that target specific sites, AMPs exhibit broad-spectrum activity by disrupting pathogen membranes or intracellular components, leading to cell death. Their versatility allows them to be integrated with advanced technologies, such as nanoparticle-based delivery systems, for clinical applications [6]. This significantly reduces the risk of emerging drug-resistant bacteria [7]. These highly diverse peptides, which leverage surface characteristics like polarity, disrupt the membranes of other organisms, ultimately inducing cell death [8]. Despite their high-antibacterial activity and functional diversity, the experimental discovery of AMPs is still hindered by efficiency and cost limitations. Therefore, an efficient computational platform that can accurately identify the antimicrobial properties of AMPs might accelerate the clinical application of AMP-based therapeutics [9].
The rapid growth of peptide datasets has spurred the creation of numerous peptide data platforms, such as the Peptide Utility search server, providing researchers with rich resources for AMP discovery [10]. Concurrently, deep learning models, combined with extensive datasets, have emerged as powerful computational tools in biological science, providing substantial savings in time and resources [11]. In recent years, AI-based approaches have been extensively applied to AMP identification [12]. For instance, tools like AMP Scanner [13], AMPfun [14], and Deep-AmPEP30 [15] utilize a diverse machine learning and deep learning techniques, including classification and regression trees [16], convolutional neural networks (CNN) [17], and long short-term memory networks [18], to analyze AMP sequences and predict their antibacterial activities. These approaches primarily focus on manipulating sequence-based features for AMP classification and functional prediction.
However, AMPs are structurally diverse polymers, categorized by their secondary structures into α-helical, β-sheet, extended/random coil, and loop (cyclic) types [19]. Sequence-based representations are often insufficient for comprehensive analysis [20]. To address this limitation, graph neural networks (GNNs) appear as a robust approach for the structural modeling of AMPs [21]. GNN effectively incorporates spatial connections and adjacent information between atoms or amino acid nodes, enabling a more holistic representation of peptides. It also allows for a comprehensive understanding of how structural variations influence the peptide’s antimicrobial activity [22]. For instance, sAMPpred-GAT [23] and esm-AxP-GDL [24] leveraged predicted peptide structures alongside GNN-based model to distinguish AMPs from non-AMPs. sAMPpred-GAT utilized trRosetta [25] for structure prediction, and then incorporated both structure and sequence information to enhance the attention-based learning for AMP classification [23]. Similarly, esm-AxP-GDL combined ESMFold-predicted structures with intermediate protein language model features extracted by ESM-2 [26] in the form of a graph-based model [24].
AMPs typically exert their antimicrobial effects by directly interacting with targets like bacterial membranes or proteins. Electrostatic attraction and hydrophobic interactions disrupt membranes or interfere with intracellular processes, ultimately causing bacterial cell death [12]. However, existing predictors did not consider the biophysical constraint and only modeled the amino acid level graph representing the whole AMP structure. We hypothesized that focusing on the functional surfaces of AMPs, particularly regions involved in protein-peptide interactions, could enhance predictions of AMP activity. Molecular Surface Interaction Fingerprinting (MaSIF) [20] provided a protocol to capture protein surfaces and compute a series of geometric and physiochemical features, including shape index, distance-dependent curvature, hydropathy, Poisson–Boltzmann continuum electrostatics, and free electrons/protons [20]. These features were extracted from AlphaFold2-predicted peptide structures, thereby supporting a more comprehensive analysis of AMP’s functional properties.
In this study, we develop a multimodal geometric deep learning framework termed SSFGM-Model. It integrates the AlphaFold2-predicted structure with the pretrained ESM-2 and ProteinBERT representations into a GNN-based architecture, further enhanced by peptide surface fingerprints, to identify functional AMPs. We collect an extensive dataset of AMP sequences and structural data, providing a basis for representing the complex characteristics of these peptides. Furthermore, we perform extensive benchmarking experiments and ablation studies to illustrate the advantages of incorporating structural and surface inputs. As a result, SSFGM-Model demonstrates superior performance in predicting AMPs compared to the existing prediction tools. It may have practical implications for the discovery of novel AMPs and the development of future antimicrobial strategies.
material and methods:
The Benchmark Dataset 1 consists of 8222 peptide sequences from three subsets: (i) 2021 AMPs and 2021 non-AMPs retrieved from the AMP Scanner vr.2 web server (www.ampscanner.com), which included the updated sequences from the APD3 [27] database; (ii) 1100 unique AMP sequences derived from the original APD3 database [27]; (iii) 1536 AMPs and 1536 non-AMPs sourced from the reference (Xu et al.). The sequences in the third subset were aggregated from various resources, including ADAM [28], ADAPTABLE [29], APD3 [27], CAMP [30], dbAMP [31], DRAMP [32, 33], LAMP [34, 35], MilkAMP [36], and YADAMP [37]. We randomly shuffled the data from the three subsets and split the dataset into training (2878 AMPs and 2600 non-AMPs), validation (895 AMPs and 656 non-AMPs), and test sets (894 AMPs and 301 non-AMPs). The length distribution of the peptide sequences is illustrated in Fig. 1b (top). AMPs are generally shorter, primarily ranging from 25 to 50 amino acids, with a consistent distribution across the training, evaluation, and test sets. In contrast, non-AMPs exhibit a wider range of sequence lengths, spanning from 25 to nearly 150 amino acids. The test set was designed to assess the model’s generalizability under the imbalanced data distribution.

The Benchmark Dataset 2 was also derived from the AMP Scanner web server [13]. Unlike the updated version in Benchmark Dataset 1, it was frequently used for model training in recent deep-learning research on AMPs. Many computational tools have benchmarked their performance on this dataset. It consists of 1778 AMP and 1778 non-AMP sequences in which AMPs were primarily sourced from the APD3 database [27], targeting Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria. To ensure data quality, we confirmed that the dataset was curated by excluding sequences shorter than 10 amino acid residues and using the CD-HIT program to remove sequences with ≥90% sequence identity. We selected 2132 sequences (1066 AMPs and 1066 non-AMPs) for training and 1424 sequences (712 AMPs and 712 non-AMPs) for testing, as shown in Fig. 1a (right), which was consistent with the data splitting setting of the existing predictors. The non-AMPs were obtained from the UniProt [38] database excluding peptides with possible antimicrobial activities in the same manner as Benchmark Dataset 1. Additionally, non-AMPs shorter than 10 amino acid residues or sharing ≥40% sequence identity were removed. The length distribution patterns of AMPs and non-AMPs in Benchmark Dataset 2 were similar to those in Benchmark Dataset 1, as illustrated in Fig. 1b (bottom). It is important to note that while some peptide sequences overlap between Benchmark Dataset 1 and Benchmark Dataset 2, the training, validation, and test sets within each dataset are entirely independent. This ensures no overlap between the training and test sets, allowing for a fair and unbiased evaluation of the model’s performance [13]. Benchmark dataset 2 was specifically used to compare our model with existing AMP predictors that were trained and tested on the same dataset.
To further investigate the impact of structure prediction tools on AMP identification, we constructed Benchmark Dataset 3, which includes 7071 AMPs and 7071 non-AMPs derived from dbAMP database [39]. This dataset was designed to evaluate how the use of ESMFold, as an alternative to AlphaFold, influences AMP prediction performance. Detailed information about Benchmark Dataset 3 is provided in Supplementary Material Text S4.
The framework of SSFGM-Model is shown in Fig. 2. The input peptide sequences were embedded as pretrained feature vectors using two advanced protein language models, ProteinBert [40] and ESM-2 [26], which represent evolutionary information, along with One-hot encodings. AlphaFold2 [41] was employed to predict the 3D structures from peptide sequences. To construct the peptide graph, amino acid residues were selected as nodes and the residue-level embeddings were used as the corresponding node features. Structural relationships between amino acid residues were captured based on the pairwise Euclidean distance between Cα atoms. Specifically, when the distance between two residue nodes was below a specific threshold (e.g. 8 Å and 10 Å in this study), an edge was established between them. The distance between residues could also serve as the edge attribute. A GNN-based network consisting of six graph convolutional network (GCN) layers and one graph attention network (GAT) layer was further utilized to perform feature propagation on the peptide graph. On the other hand, we referred to MaSIF [20] to extract geometric features (shape index and distance-dependent curvature) and chemical features (hydropathy index, continuum electrostatics, and locations of free electrons and proton donors) [20] from the peptide surface patches. These features were mapped onto the geodesic polar coordinates to describe the relative positions within the local surface patch. The geometric neural network was subsequently applied to the learning the underlying biophysical representations. Finally, the model fused the outputs of the two subnetworks to enhance the prediction for antimicrobial activity.

In addition to the SSFGM-Model, we developed a sequence-feature-based model, SEQC-Model (Sequence-based CNN Model), which integrated sequence information using a two-layer CNN. Two structure-based models were also established in this study: (i) SSGT-Model (Sequence and Structure-based GCN-Transformer Model) combining three GCN layers, two transformer layers with eight heads, and two GAT layers; (ii) SSGA-Model (Sequence and Structure-based GCN with Attention Model) employing six GCN layers and a single GAT layer. These models were all evaluated to assess the contribution of the key components in the SSFGM model.

We employed the ColabFold [46] version of AlphaFold2 [41] to predict the three-dimensional structures of all peptide sequences in our dataset, generating corresponding Protein Data Bank (PDB) files containing atomic coordinates of the peptides, where a PDB file is a standard text format used to represent the three-dimensional structure of biological macromolecules [47]. Graphs were constructed based on these coordinates where the edges represent potential interactions between amino acid residues, such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds, and van der Waals forces [48]. The three-dimensional coordinates provide information about the distances between amino acid residues, reflecting their spatial interactions [49]. Thus, we extracted the three-dimensional coordinates of each peptide sequence from the predicted structure with the highest predicted Local Distance Difference Test (pLDDT) score [41]. The positions of the Cα atoms in all standard amino acids were selected to represent the residue-level coordinates. Next, edges were constructed in the graph based on the Euclidean distances between residues. By calculating the distances and applying a threshold (10 Å or 8 Å in this study), we determined whether an undirected edge should be established between two amino acid residues. The corresponding distance was also included as an edge attribute. This approach enabled the graph to reflect spatial proximity between residues, helping the GNN-based network capture structural interactions within the peptide.
With regard to the node features, we combined the sequence-level feature vectors, including One-hot encoding, ProteinBERT embeddings, and ESM-2 embeddings. Each node represented an amino acid residue, with its sequence features, while the edges captured the spatial interactions between residues. Using this approach, we generated peptide graphs that incorporate both sequence and structural information, which were used to train the graph neural network for AMP classification.
The geometric and chemical features for each vertex on the protein surface were extracted from the three-dimensional structures of peptide sequences predicted by AlphaFold2. Each peptide covered several surface patches with a geodesic radius of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{upgreek} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document} $r=12$\end{document}Å and 100 vertices [20], And each vertex was characterized by five geometric or physiochemical properties: shape index, distance-dependent curvature, Poisson–Boltzmann continuum electrostatics, free electrons and proton donors, and hydropathy [20].
The shape index represents the local geometric shape of each vertex, indicating the degree of concavity or convexity [50]. The closer the shape index value is to −1, the more concave the vertex is, while the closer it is to +1, the more convex the vertex is [20].
Distance-dependent curvature represents the relationship between the distance from a vertex to the patch center and the surface normal at those points [50]. This relationship is expressed as a curvature value, reflecting the relative geometric shape between the vertex and the center. When the curvature value approaches −0.7, the region around the vertex is concave relative to the patch center; when the value approaches +0.7, the vertex is more convex compared to the patch center [20].
Poisson–Boltzmann continuum electrostatics is used to numerically represent the electrostatic properties of vertex on the meshed surface of the protein (Adaptive Poisson–Boltzmann Solver), Values closer to −1 indicate stronger negative charge at the vertex, while values closer to +1 indicate stronger positive charge [20].
Free electrons and proton donors describe the potential of a protein surface vertex to act as a hydrogen bond donor or acceptor. Calculating the likelihood of each vertex being a free electron (hydrogen bond acceptor) or proton donor (hydrogen bond donor) helps the model identify regions on the protein surface that may participate in intermolecular interactions. Values closer to −1 indicate an optimal hydrogen bond acceptor site, while values closer to +1 indicate an optimal hydrogen bond donor site [20].
The calculation of hydropathy is crucial for analyzing protein surface features. In this study, the hydropathy values are assigned to each vertex based on the Kyte and Doolittle scale of amino acid hydrophobicity [51]. The initial range of values is [−4.5, +4.5], which is then normalized to the range of [−1, +1]. In this normalized scale, values closer to −1 indicate a more hydrophilic vertex, while values closer to +1 indicate a more hydrophobic vertex [20].
The geodesic polar coordinates of each vertex included the radial coordinate and angular coordinate. The radial coordinate represented the distance from each vertex to the center of the patch, while the angular coordinate represented the direction of each vertex relative to the center. These vertex-based coordinates could capture not only the spatial features and geometric shape of each vertex but also their relative position to the patch center, laying the foundation for subsequent computations in the geometric neural network [20].
The GNN subnetwork in the SSFGM-Model consisted of three main components: GCN layers, GAT layers, and fully connected layers, as illustrated in Fig. 2b. We first concatenated three different embedding methods to create a 3604-dimensional feature for each node. Six consecutive GCN layers were used to propagate and update information from each node and its adjacent nodes through a weighted average aggregation. The impact of different GCN layer depths on model performance was systematically evaluated, as shown in Tables S6-1 and S6-2. They also progressively reduced the dimension of node features. It is implemented by combining the node’s own features with a weighted average of its neighboring nodes’ features.

The GNN model architecture enabled effective learning of biological feature representation while reducing the data dimensionality. Node features were further aggregated into graph-level global features using global mean pooling, and then passed through fully connected layers to learn discriminative feature vectors.
The geometric convolutional network in this study was based on the method described in the reference [20]. This model could interpret interaction fingerprints on protein molecular surfaces by integrating geometric and chemical features through geometric deep learning techniques. It identified surface structures by calculating shape index and distance-dependent curvature and detected interaction sites according to hydrophobicity index, electrostatic continuity, as well as the positions of free electrons and proton donors. Additionally, it utilized geodesic radius coordinates and central angular coordinates to pinpoint the positions of surface vertices.
The model employed Gaussian activation functions and rotation invariance techniques to perform multiple rotations [52]. After each rotation, it recalculated the spatial relationship between surface points and the central point and adjusted the angular coordinates accordingly. Gaussian functions were used to assign weights to each vertex, and features were aggregated across both rotations and vertices. Finally, these features were transformed through a fully connected layer. This rotation-invariant design ensured that key geometric and chemical features could be accurately captured, regardless of changes in the orientation of the protein surface.
To achieve our goal of recognizing AMPs, we employed a multimodal approach that integrated sequence, structure, and surface information through feature fusion (see the supplement file for more information). The fusion method combined output features from the GNN-based network and the geometric neural network. After feature extraction and concatenation, a ReLU activation function was employed to introduce nonlinear transformations, enhancing the model’s ability to learn complex patterns. Subsequently, these processed features were fed to a linear layer and finally passed through a log softmax function to ensure the outputs could be interpreted as a probability distribution. A probability closer to 1 suggests the presence of an AMP, while a probability closer to 0 indicates a non-AMP.
For training the SSFGM-Model, the batch size was set to 32. The cross-entropy loss function [53] was employed for the classification task, while the AdamW optimizer [54] (with an initial learning rate of 0.0001 and a weight decay of 1e-2) was applied to update model parameters. Learning rate scheduling was managed using a combination of cosine annealing schedule [55] and reducing learning rate when a metric has stopped improving [56]. The learning rate was dynamically adjusted using a cosine annealing schedule over 10 epochs, with additional reductions triggered when the validation loss plateaued. Specifically, the learning rate was decreased by a factor of 0.1 after a patience period of 5 epochs. The model was trained for a total of 60 epochs, and a dropout rate of 0.5 was applied after each convolutional layer to mitigate overfitting. Training was performed on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU, utilizing CUDA version 11.3, PyTorch version 1.12.1 [57], and Python version 3.10.12.
In this study, we evaluated three feature fusion techniques: direct concatenation of outputs from both models, linear transformation of the output features to a uniform dimension followed by concatenation, and postlinear transformation and concatenation using multihead attention mechanisms to selectively emphasize features more relevant to the task. The feature fusion techniques are described in detail in Supplementary Text S1–S3, and the results are shown in Tables S1 and S2. We assessed the performance under the best concatenation methods and have provided a detailed discussion in the “Result and Discussion” section of this paper.
We employed multiple classification metrics to evaluate the performance of the model, including accuracy (ACC), sensitivity (SN), specificity (SP), precision (PR), Matthews’ correlation coefficient (MCC), area under the ROC curve (AUC), and area under the precision-recall curve. ACC assesses the overall performance of the model in distinguishing AMPs (positive class) from non-AMPs (negative class). AUC provides a more comprehensive evaluation of the model’s ability to separate positive and negative samples. The ROC curve illustrates the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity at various classification thresholds, where a higher AUC indicates stronger discriminatory power between antimicrobial and non-AMPs.
The metrics are derived from TP (true positives), TN (true negatives), FP (false positives), and FN (false negatives), which collectively contribute to the evaluation. In cases of class imbalance, MCC offers a more reliable performance assessment by considering all four components (TP, TN, FP, FN), making it a better metric than ACC in such scenarios.

the overview of ssfgm model:
The framework of SSFGM-Model is shown in Fig. 2. The input peptide sequences were embedded as pretrained feature vectors using two advanced protein language models, ProteinBert [40] and ESM-2 [26], which represent evolutionary information, along with One-hot encodings. On the other hand, we referred to MaSIF [20] to extract geometric features (shape index and distance-dependent curvature) and chemical features (hydropathy index, continuum electrostatics, and locations of free electrons and proton donors) [20] from the peptide surface patches. These features were mapped onto the geodesic polar coordinates to describe the relative positions within the local surface patch. The geometric neural network was subsequently applied to the learning the underlying biophysical representations. Finally, the model fused the outputs of the two subnetworks to enhance the prediction for antimicrobial activity.

hydropathy: The calculation of hydropathy is crucial for analyzing protein surface features. In this study, the hydropathy values are assigned to each vertex based on the Kyte and Doolittle scale of amino acid hydrophobicity [51]. The initial range of values is [−4.5, +4.5], which is then normalized to the range of [−1, +1]. In this normalized scale, values closer to −1 indicate a more hydrophilic vertex, while values closer to +1 indicate a more hydrophobic vertex [20].
geodesic polar coordinates: The geodesic polar coordinates of each vertex included the radial coordinate and angular coordinate. The radial coordinate represented the distance from each vertex to the center of the patch, while the angular coordinate represented the direction of each vertex relative to the center. These vertex-based coordinates could capture not only the spatial features and geometric shape of each vertex but also their relative position to the patch center, laying the foundation for subsequent computations in the geometric neural network [20].

The geometric convolutional network in this study was based on the method described in the reference [20]. This model could interpret interaction fingerprints on protein molecular surfaces by integrating geometric and chemical features through geometric deep learning techniques. It identified surface structures by calculating shape index and distance-dependent curvature and detected interaction sites according to hydrophobicity index, electrostatic continuity, as well as the positions of free electrons and proton donors. Additionally, it utilized geodesic radius coordinates and central angular coordinates to pinpoint the positions of surface vertices.
The model employed Gaussian activation functions and rotation invariance techniques to perform multiple rotations [52]. After each rotation, it recalculated the spatial relationship between surface points and the central point and adjusted the angular coordinates accordingly. Gaussian functions were used to assign weights to each vertex, and features were aggregated across both rotations and vertices. Finally, these features were transformed through a fully connected layer. This rotation-invariant design ensured that key geometric and chemical features could be accurately captured, regardless of changes in the orientation of the protein surface.
To achieve our goal of recognizing AMPs, we employed a multimodal approach that integrated sequence, structure, and surface information through feature fusion (see the supplement file for more information). The fusion method combined output features from the GNN-based network and the geometric neural network. After feature extraction and concatenation, a ReLU activation function was employed to introduce nonlinear transformations, enhancing the model’s ability to learn complex patterns. Subsequently, these processed features were fed to a linear layer and finally passed through a log softmax function to ensure the outputs could be interpreted as a probability distribution. A probability closer to 1 suggests the presence of an AMP, while a probability closer to 0 indicates a non-AMP.
For training the SSFGM-Model, the batch size was set to 32. The cross-entropy loss function [53] was employed for the classification task, while the AdamW optimizer [54] (with an initial learning rate of 0.0001 and a weight decay of 1e-2) was applied to update model parameters. Learning rate scheduling was managed using a combination of cosine annealing schedule [55] and reducing learning rate when a metric has stopped improving [56]. The learning rate was dynamically adjusted using a cosine annealing schedule over 10 epochs, with additional reductions triggered when the validation loss plateaued. Specifically, the learning rate was decreased by a factor of 0.1 after a patience period of 5 epochs. The model was trained for a total of 60 epochs, and a dropout rate of 0.5 was applied after each convolutional layer to mitigate overfitting. Training was performed on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU, utilizing CUDA version 11.3, PyTorch version 1.12.1 [57], and Python version 3.10.12.
In this study, we evaluated three feature fusion techniques: direct concatenation of outputs from both models, linear transformation of the output features to a uniform dimension followed by concatenation, and postlinear transformation and concatenation using multihead attention mechanisms to selectively emphasize features more relevant to the task. The feature fusion techniques are described in detail in Supplementary Text S1–S3, and the results are shown in Tables S1 and S2. We assessed the performance under the best concatenation methods and have provided a detailed discussion in the “Result and Discussion” section of this paper.
We employed multiple classification metrics to evaluate the performance of the model, including accuracy (ACC), sensitivity (SN), specificity (SP), precision (PR), Matthews’ correlation coefficient (MCC), area under the ROC curve (AUC), and area under the precision-recall curve. ACC assesses the overall performance of the model in distinguishing AMPs (positive class) from non-AMPs (negative class). AUC provides a more comprehensive evaluation of the model’s ability to separate positive and negative samples. The ROC curve illustrates the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity at various classification thresholds, where a higher AUC indicates stronger discriminatory power between antimicrobial and non-AMPs.
The metrics are derived from TP (true positives), TN (true negatives), FP (false positives), and FN (false negatives), which collectively contribute to the evaluation. In cases of class imbalance, MCC offers a more reliable performance assessment by considering all four components (TP, TN, FP, FN), making it a better metric than ACC in such scenarios.

Firstly, we conducted a comparative analysis to evaluate the impact of varying distance thresholds, the number of GCN layers [58], and transformer layers [59] on the predictive performance of our models. Benchmark Dataset 1 was used for this comparison, and the results are summarized in Table 1. Specifically, we examined distance thresholds of 8 Å and 10 Å, as these values are often utilized to capture meaningful structural proximity in molecular interactions [60]. Two deep learning architectures (SSGT-Model and SSGA-Model) were compared in this study. For a fair and consistent comparison, both models were trained for 30 epochs, ensuring an equitable assessment of their predictive capabilities.
Performance comparison of different structure-based models under varying thresholds.
Figure 3a presents the performance metrics—ACC, AUC, MCC, SENS, and SPEC—obtained by the models using two network architectures with distance thresholds set at 8 Å and 10 Å. Notably, when employing an architecture that combines three GCN layers, two transformer layers with eight heads, and two GAT layers (SSGT-Model), the model with a 10 Å distance threshold exhibited superior performance, achieving an ACC of 0.8871, an AUC of 0.8897, and an MCC of 0.7731. These metrics surpassed those of the corresponding model with an 8 Å distance threshold, which achieved an ACC of 0.8774, an AUC of 0.8807, and an MCC of 0.7545. A similar trend was observed with architecture incorporating six GCN layers and a single GAT layer. The model using a 10 Å distance threshold outperformed the 8 Å model, achieving an ACC of 0.8929, an AUC of 0.9547, and an MCC of 0.7854, compared to the 8 Å model’s ACC of 0.8871, AUC of 0.8897, and MCC of 0.7731. In particular, the AUC values for the 10 Å models substantially exceeded those of the 8 Å models. This marked improvement in predictive performance at the 10 Å distance threshold highlighted its ability to capture molecular interactions. Therefore, we selected the 10 Å distance threshold for subsequent model comparisons and evaluations, as it clearly provides a more effective representation for improving prediction outcomes.

Additionally, we compared the performance of the two model architectures (SSGA-Model and SSGT-Model). The results demonstrate that the architecture with six GCN layers and a single attention layer significantly outperformed the three-GCN-layer Transformer-based model. As shown in Table 1, at a distance threshold of 8 Å, the six-GCN-layer model achieved a higher AUC of 0.8897 and an ACC of 0.8774, compared to the Transformer-based model’s AUC of 0.8807 and ACC of 0.8871. When the distance threshold was increased to 10 Å, the six-GCN-layer model further excelled, achieving an AUC of 0.9547 and an ACC of 0.8929, clearly surpassing the Transformer-based model, which had an AUC of 0.9137 and an ACC of 0.8875. These findings highlighted the advantage of using deeper GCN layers in combination with a GAT layer to boost predictive performance for this task. Consequently, we selected the six-GCN-layer architecture with a single GAT layer as the final module in further evaluations.
In summary, both the distance threshold and network architecture played critical roles in determining predictive accuracy. The 10 Å distance threshold consistently yielded superior results across different models, and the architecture with six GCN layers and a GAT layer outperformed the more complex Transformer-based model.
As mentioned above, we employed five types of peptide representation features as inputs to our model, including One-hot encodings, ProteinBERT encodings, ESM encodings, structure information of peptides (contact maps), and protein surface features derived from the AlphaFold2-predicted 3D structures. To investigate the combined contributions of these features to predictive performance, we first conducted a series of comparisons using various feature combinations based on Benchmark Dataset 1. Each model was trained for 50 epochs, and the results are summarized in Table 2 and Fig. 3b. Our results demonstrated that utilizing ProteinBERT, One-hot, and ESM-2 encodings through a network with two CNN layers (SEQC) achieved an AUC of 0.9415 and an ACC of 0.8768. Additionally, incorporating structural contact maps to construct peptide graphs, along with ProteinBERT, One-hot, and ESM encodings as node features through GCN layers (SSGA), further improved the model performance. The architecture with six GCN layers and a single GAT layer resulted in an AUC of 0.9547, an ACC of 0.8929, and an MCC of 0.7854. Meanwhile, an architecture (SSGT) comprising three GCN layers, two transformer layers with eight heads, and two GAT layers yielded an ACC of 0.8875 and an MCC of 0.7745, although the AUC was slightly lower (0.9137). These findings underscore the importance of incorporating both sequence and structural information to improve the model capacity.

conclusions:
In this study, we have comprehensively extracted multilevel characteristics of AMPs and compared model built on these features to elucidate the significant contributions of structural and surface geometric chemical properties in AMP identification. Our results demonstrate that deep learning models incorporating structural and surface features significantly outperform those based on traditional feature extraction methods. This work represents the first multimodal fusion of surface biochemical properties and geometric characteristics with an advanced protein language model at both the sequence and structural levels. Furthermore, we applied a geometric neural network alongside this fusion to predict AMPs, providing a novel methodology that integrates evolutionary, structural, geometric, and biochemical information of peptide sequences. Our findings underscore the efficacy of graph and geometric neural networks in AMP prediction, highlighting their potential for processing high-dimensional, complex biological data.
Nonetheless, several practical challenges remain. While ESM and ProteinBERT embeddings provide rich residue-specific features at the sequence level, they generate high-dimensional vectors that demand significant memory and computational resources. Additionally, structural predictions (via AlphaFold or ESMFold) and surface geometric physicochemical feature extraction (using MaSIF) substantially increase computational complexity and processing time. Moreover, although the current model excels at identifying AMPs, it lacks the granularity required to distinguish specific functional classes, limiting its direct applicability for detailed functional characterization. Despite these limitations, our integrated multilevel feature approach significantly enhances predictive accuracy and robustness.
Looking ahead, we plan to leverage this model to explore peptides with potentially unannotated/unlabeled antimicrobial properties, while extending its capability to differentiate between distinct AMP functional classes. Additionally, we also aim to integrate advanced generative models to design novel AMPs based on their sequence, structure, and surface features. Concurrently, we will optimize the feature extraction pipeline to improve computational efficiency and reduce memory requirements. These advancements will facilitate the development of peptides with targeted antibacterial activity and enhanced potency, accelerating the clinical translation of AMPs and inspiring innovative strategies for antimicrobial drug discovery.
